Choked
chōkt
v. (stopped, smothered; the word of the parable for a word that is prevented from bearing fruit)
Middle English choken, to stop the breath. The Greek sumpnigo is a compound — to press together and strangle — used of thorns around wheat and of a crowd pressing about Christ.

Biblical Definition

The word belongs to the parable of the sower, where it names the third soil and the most respectable failure. “And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them” (Mat 13:7); Mark adds the outcome, “and it yielded no fruit” (Mar 4:7). The Lord Himself supplies the interpretation, and it is remarkable for containing nothing scandalous: “And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection” (Luk 8:14). Matthew names two of the three: “the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful” (Mat 13:22). Not persecution, not heresy, not open sin — anxiety, money and pleasure, all three of them ordinary. The same verb is used of the swine at Gadara, which “ran violently down a steep place into the sea… and were choked in the sea” (Mar 5:13). Thorns do not attack the seed; they simply grow in the same ground, and take the light.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to choke as to stop the passage of the breath; to suffocate; and figuratively, to obstruct, to stop, to hinder or check the growth of anything.

expand to see more

CHOKE, v.t. To stop the passage of the breath, by filling the windpipe or compressing the neck; to suffocate; to stifle.

2. To stop by filling; to obstruct; to block up; as, to choke a passage.

3. To hinder or check growth, expansion or progress. The thorns sprung up and choked them. Matt. xiii.

4. To smother or suffocate, as fire.

Key Scripture

Mat 13:7 — "And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them:"

Luk 8:14 — "And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection."

Mat 13:22 — "He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful."

Mar 4:7 — "And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up, and choked it, and it yielded no fruit."

Modern Corruption

The thorny ground is preached as a warning against gross sin, when the Lord names cares, riches and pleasures — three things a respectable congregation will not call sins at all.

expand to see more

Nothing in the Lord's own interpretation of the thorns is disreputable. Cares is anxiety about real matters — a mortgage, a diagnosis, a child. Riches is money, described as deceitful rather than as evil, because its lie is that it can secure what only God secures. Pleasures of this life are lawful enjoyments. Not one of the three would be named in a testimony as the thing that ruined a man, and that is precisely why the Lord names them. A hearer is not choked by an obvious rival; he is choked by a hundred legitimate things growing in the same soil until there is no room left. And the outcome is not apostasy with a bang but a slow unfruitfulness: he brings no fruit to perfection, which is to say the growth begins and is never completed.

It is worth being exact about what the parable does and does not prove. The thorny ground is not a picture of a true believer losing his salvation; the same Lord who spoke this parable said that of all the Father gave Him He should lose nothing. It is a picture of a hearing that never came to fruit, and Scripture's consistent mark of genuine life is fruit that appears and continues, however slowly. The pastoral use is therefore self-examination rather than the sorting of other men into soils. A Christian may ask, plainly, which of the three is growing in his ground this year, and act on the answer — for thorns are not removed by resolving to bear fruit but by being pulled up. Christ Himself wore a crown of them, which is the ground of any hope that the field can be cleared at all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sumpnigo (G4846), to press together and strangle; with merimna (G3308), care or anxiety, apate ploutou (G539, G4149), the deceitfulness of riches, and hedone (G2237), pleasure.

expand to see more

Greek sumpnigo (G4846) — to choke utterly, to press together; of the thorns and of the crowd thronging Christ; Luke 8:14, Luke 8:42.

Greek merimna (G3308) — care, anxiety, a divided mind; the first thorn; Matthew 13:22, 1 Peter 5:7.

Greek apate (G539) — deceit; joined to riches, which promise a security they cannot give; Matthew 13:22.

Greek hedone (G2237) — pleasure, gratification; the third thorn, and the root of the English hedonism; Luke 8:14, James 4:3.

Greek telesphoreo (G5052) — to bring to completion or perfection; what the choked hearer never does with fruit; Luke 8:14.

Usage

"“The thorns sprung up, and choked them” — no attack, only the same ground and the light taken."

"“Choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life” — three things nobody confesses."

"“Bring no fruit to perfection” — growth begun and never completed."
